Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with many models from popular brands like Dyson and Shark starting at $1,200. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and with early Black Friday deals already kicking off, it's one of the best times to shop for one.
One of our favorite robot vacuum brands, Roborock , began its early Black Friday deals yesterday, and some of our favorite models we've tested are available for the best prices we've seen. Here's which models I'd snatch up while the prices are low.
The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro launched in late summer as the newest addition to the brand's more affordable Qrevo line, and it quickly landed as a pick on my guide to the Best Robot Vacuums . It's often on sale for around $600, and thanks to Black Friday it's down to the lowest price I've seen it for: $450, nearly half off.
Overall, Roborock's vacuums are great, but I've been especially impressed by this one's corner cleaning, thanks to its extendable mop arm. It won't always spot cords, but it does a better job at navigating furniture and getting underneath my cabinets than more expensive robot vacuums I've tested.
If you'd rather have a roller-mop-style robot vacuum, the Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is another great option from Roborock's Qrevo line. This one came out in January of this year, and our reviewer instantly loved it .
The Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is a more expensive robot vacuum than the Qrevo 2 since it comes with the brand's SpriaFlow roller-mop. The internal roller spans nearly the entire width of the vacuum and can extend to edge-clean your home. It even has a built-in scraper to move dirty water into the tank instead of rolling it back onto the floor. If you're looking for an affordable mopping powerhouse, this is the one to choose. It's also nearly half off, down to $600 off the $1,000 price tag.
There's the affordable Qrevo line from Roborock, and then there's the higher-end Saros line. While both I and former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So weren't particularly impressed with the Saros 20, I've been much happier with the performance of the Saros 20 Flow. Like the Curv 2 Flow, it has a roller mop instead of spinning mop pads and did well in my mopping tests. It also didn't leave debris around, even with its high suction of 36,000 Pa.
It's one of Roborock's most expensive vacuums, and it comes across while using it—it feels very premium. I've been preferring it over the new Dyson robot vacuum I've been testing. Luckily, you can get it on sale right now for Black Friday. It still isn't cheap at $1,300, but it's one of my all-time favorites and one I have kept coming back to after trying other models.
If you're looking for something truly unique in a robot vacuum, Roborock's Saros Z70 might be what you're looking for. It has a mechanical arm built into it to pick up small items like socks while it vacuums, which feels handy, but didn't work as well as we'd hoped during testing. Still, maybe you feel that's the solution you've been dying for. If that's the case, it's available for a nice discount right now at $950.
It also packs 22,000 Pa of suction (not as powerful as the Saros 20 Flow, but still plenty of suction to clean carpets and rugs alike!) and still executes fast, effective cleaning. But the battery life on this vacuum isn't as long as that of other Roborocks we've tested. Again, you're mostly getting this one for the mechanical arm.

Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.
The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.
Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.
An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.
The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.
Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.
Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.
Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop to refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.
XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.
Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.
Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.
The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO 2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO 2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.
In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.
Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.
As with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO 2 -cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.
That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

METR’s latest report finds that AI models are still improving at a rapid clip, but they show some weaknesses in tasks that require judgment.
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.
The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.
It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.
And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.
METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.
In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.
Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”
Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.
Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.
Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.
But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”
Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”
In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.
In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.
It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.
Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.
The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.
The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.
Gemini for Home was announced last year , so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year ). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar , the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.
Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . Under his leadership, billions of dollars ’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two ?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.
Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.
It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?
The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.
At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.
Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justifies-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.
The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a company have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail ?)
There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public company, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.
On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession plan. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he said. “If a company will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”
Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.
Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

Agreements aim to simplify trade checks, link emissions systems and launch a youth mobility programme.
The United Kingdom and the European Union have struck a deal aimed at mending fences and repairing the economic fallout caused by Brexit, a decade after UK voters opted to leave the bloc.
At a joint news conference following the EU-UK summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the deal would “rebuild the bridges that were broken all those years ago”. He hailed the agreements as “a good deal for Britain”.
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, said there was an “intensive” debate on how much the world has changed since Brexit, during the meeting.
The COVID pandemic “was not even over when Russia started the war in Ukraine”, she said. “We have stuck together from day one on.
“We can always work on an incremental improvement of our relationship, but as I said, we are totally open to do the necessary brainstorming for the wider picture.”
The agreements cover three areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies.
But disagreements remain, particularly over university tuition fees.
Burnham also faces political resistance at home over how far strengthening ties with the EU should go.
Three main agreements were on the table at the summit between Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
The first would remove checks and reduce paperwork on food and agricultural products traded between Britain and the EU, making exports easier and potentially lowering costs for businesses and consumers. That could be good news for businesspeople like Tim Jones , an English cheesemaker whom Al Jazeera recently interviewed.
The second would link the two sides’ emissions-trading systems, which would give an exemption to goods from Britain and the EU, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The third establishes a youth mobility programme allowing up to 100,000 people under 30 from each side to live in the other’s territory for up to three years for work, study or travel.
Burnham said the agreements could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s gross domestic product (GDP), raising his previous estimate of 0.4 percent.
The prime minister described the package as a way of “cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people”.
Despite the breakthrough, hurdles remain, among them university tuition fees. Brussels wants EU students attending British universities to pay the same domestic rates as British students rather than the substantially higher international fees currently charged.
London has resisted the proposal, which could have significant financial implications for universities.
“We have not yet reached an agreement on tuition fees, and we have given ourselves six months to reach that agreement,” an EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters.
Another unresolved issue concerns Britain’s demand for access to the EU’s “made in Europe” rules, notably for cars.
“Made in Europe” is part of the EU’s planned Industrial Accelerator Act and is aimed primarily at forcing Chinese automakers to produce cars within the bloc using local suppliers in order to qualify for key subsidies and bid for government procurement contracts.
The EU has indicated it is willing to grant this but on the condition that London aligns with its policies, which restrict imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
Burnham has indicated that his government will examine longer-term options, ranging from maintaining existing arrangements to joining the EU customs union or eventually rejoining the bloc.
“After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship,” he said.
But rejoining would require support from British voters and unanimous approval from EU member states, making any immediate return unlikely.
Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from Brussels, said there was “no actual signing” expected on Friday. “There’s no document being inked,” she said.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera, “As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place … and talks will continue on some areas.”
Within Burnham’s Labour Party, some politicians support rebuilding European ties but fear reopening the divisive Brexit debate.
“I’m happy with closer ties, but he does need to tread carefully,” one Labour MP told the AFP news agency.
The opposition Conservatives and Nigel Farage’s Reform UK have predictably criticised the government’s direction. “I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again,” Farage, who led the Brexit campaign, told the BBC.
He warned that the discussion would soon become one about whether Britain should rejoin the EU.
A YouGov poll published on Wednesday suggested 54 percent of UK citizens think “it would be acceptable to have a rejoin referendum in the next five years” but are divided over whether it is a top priority.
European officials, meanwhile, have remained cautious about Britain’s longer-term intentions.
Sonja Hyland, Ireland’s ambassador in London, said there was “a lack of clarity” about what Brexit meant. If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must “make a clear decision as to what it wants”.

Staffers at the Internet Archive , the nonprofit “ digital library ” that runs the Wayback Machine , are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA).
More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. Kahle did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.
The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996 . Kahle’s mission was to provide “Universal Access to All Knowledge.” Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how “aligned” employees are in their passion for Kahle’s goals.
“Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle’s] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge,” Howes tells WIRED.
Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard tells WIRED that the union is “very optimistic” that Kahle will voluntarily recognize it and come to the bargaining table. They add that among the union’s core goals are securing wage increases and additional benefits, and ensuring that these benefits are consistently available to employees across the company.
“We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive,” Leard says.
Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive—which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages—employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive’s building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff’s diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, “a unique challenge,” but one that’s “really rewarding.”
The vote comes slightly more than two months after staffers at the Wikimedia Foundation , the nonprofit behind Wikipedia, voted to join CWA. Howes says the simultaneous efforts are “very powerful” given that both organizations represent “core infrastructure” of the internet.
Howes says that the union wants to ensure that the 30-year-old project continues to thrive in the long term—and that its workers do too. Leard says this means providing paths for developing skills and getting promoted within the nonprofit.
Leard says that the Internet Archive’s unionization drive is especially important in the present moment, amid waves of tech layoffs and widespread anxiety about “emerging technologies” like AI .
The Internet Archive hasn’t been immune from the consequences of AI. A Nieman Lab report from January found that some news websites, struggling to prevent companies like OpenAI or Anthropic from harvesting their articles, have started blocking web crawlers from the Internet Archive, arguing it gives AI companies a back door to their content. (The archive relies on web crawlers to preserve news articles in near-real time.)
Leard says that ideally, the Internet Archive’s unionization will be “one domino” in a larger process that makes the tech industry better.
“We're hoping,” they say, “that we'll continue to be one of the blueprints that will make it easier for other organizations and companies in the future to continue to unionize.”
Update: 11/20/26 1:43pm ET: This story has been updated to reflect that Internet Archive workers have voted in favor of unionizing, but the union has not yet been recognized by Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle.

The European Union and the United Kingdom have agreed on "landmark" deals on youth mobility and trade. Leaders on both sides praised the agreement as they seek to rebuild ties.
European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.
"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.
Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.
He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."
Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances."
He went further and said " Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.
Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."
She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."
Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.
She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."
Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it."
In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.
No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students
"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.
Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,."
On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.
They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.
According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.
Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues.
The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.

On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit .
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

As talks are held in Brussels over closer relations, we examine the economic context and the challenges ahead
The UK and EU will hold the second summit since Brexit on Friday against a volatile economic backdrop.
Taking place in Brussels as the war in the Middle East hits the global economy, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will meet the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen , and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
Burnham has said that Brexit “has not worked”, citing damage to the UK economy from leaving the bloc. However, there are also economic challenges facing the EU. Here we spell out the economic context behind the talks.
After the 2016 Brexit vote, years of political turmoil and economic uncertainty damaged business investment. Trade has also been hit by new barriers and red tape for exporters under the Brexit deal agreed by Boris Johnson.
Analysis by the economist Nick Bloom shows that UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a 4% hit over a 15-year period.
UK services trade has fared better. UK goods exports to the EU in 2025 were 14% below 2019 in real terms. Exports outside the EU were 8% lower. Services exports were 28% higher to the EU and 26% higher elsewhere, fuelled by Britain’s dominant financial services sector, as well as travel, accountancy, law, professional services, telecommunications and IT.
Britain has conducted trade policy independently of Brussels since Brexit. This has helped and hindered the UK in different ways. The government has been able to cut tariffs on certain products to help households with rising living costs – including gherkins in last month’s budget. The UK also struck a tariff deal with Donald Trump on better terms than managed by the EU . However, critics say the UK lacks the clout it had as part of the EU to sign international deals, and that sharply diverging from EU policies is undesirable. This is because divergence could undermine trading relations with the UK’s single largest trade partner.
The UK has taken a greater lead in AI adoption than EU nations, ranking third in the Global AI Index . France is the highest-ranked EU nation, in sixth. This is in part – but not entirely – down to the UK taking a lighter-touch approach to regulation than Brussels.
So far this year the UK has grown at the second-fastest pace in the G7, as AI bolsters growth despite headwinds from the war in the Middle East.
Brexit also had consequences for the EU, although as a larger market the changes have not been as profound. Barriers to trade have made Britain harder to access for EU exporters and migration has fallen.
Brexit gave a boost to populist political movements in EU countries. A wave of copycat exits did not materialise, with Britain’s political turmoil and economic uncertainty serving as a deterrent . But support for populist Eurosceptic parties remains, and battles over immigration, sovereignty and democratic accountability have not gone away.
The EU economy has faced similar global challenges to the UK – including from the 2022 Russian energy price shock and war in the Middle East. Trump has also aggressively targeted the EU in his tariff war.
Germany in particular has struggled from surging energy costs and Chinese competition hitting its industrial base. France has faced mounting political uncertainty, driving up borrowing costs and hitting growth.
Some EU economies have boomed – including former eastern bloc countries such as Poland, which has benefited from EU membership. Southern European economies at the heart of the 2010s eurozone debt crisis have also staged a marked turnaround.
The latest forecasts from the European Commission show that, as in Britain, the EU economy has proven more resilient than feared to the Middle East war. Germany has raised investment spending, particularly on defence, in response to Trump ripping up the western security consensus. AI-related investment has also bolstered activity.
For the UK there will be infighting over the extent of ambition for the future EU relationship. This could fuel uncertainty for businesses and take up political and civil service bandwidth that could have been deployed elsewhere.
Rejoining the EU would not mean a return to 2016. Some UK involvement in EU supply chains may have gone permanently. Investors may remain nervous about British commitments to EU relations – particularly as the next general election draws near.
However, most experts are clear that there would be economic benefits from closer relations. Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimate that rejoining the single market could grow the UK economy by 2-5%, equivalent to £61bn to £152bn by the start of the next decade.
The focus at this UK-EU summit will be on a youth mobility scheme , a food and drink trade deal that could add up to £5.1bn a year to the UK economy, and an emissions linking agreement that could add £3.8bn a year.
The EU will face a series of critical elections next year, including in France, Poland and Italy. Populism is on the rise and Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls to become the next French president. Germany does not have elections until 2029 but the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party is gaining support.
Early next year there also will be a test for the EU with the appointment of a new president of the European Central Bank to replace Christine Lagarde . That will come against a backdrop of rising inflationary pressures, slowing economic growth and pressures on government borrowing costs. The Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos is considered the frontrunner.
Britain is also expected to face a tougher year in 2027 due to the impact of high inflation from the war in the Middle East, with the squeeze on households also expected to weigh on growth.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
A decade after the narrow vote to leave the EU, the United Kingdom is showing every sign of buyer’s remorse.
For many, the bitterly fought contest over the referendum on whether to leave the EU was unpleasant and divisive.
Couples and families reportedly split over where they stood on the referendum. Each side of the debate – Leave and Remain – became a cipher for how people saw themselves and their country in a changing world.
As the campaign unfolded amid accusations of foreign influence and dirty tricks, the murder of a politician , a debate over economics and political sovereignty, a visceral fight intensified over identity, belonging and competing visions of what it meant to be British.
Critics and pro-Brexit slammed various exit deals that successive governments negotiated with Brussels as somehow a betrayal of what had originally been a binary choice.
The EU, the trading bloc the UK sat uneasily within for nearly half a century, remains the country’s biggest trading partner.
On Friday, in a joint news conference with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, following the latest UK-EU summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the first in a series of expected deals with the EU as rebuilding “the bridges that were broken all those years ago”.
The agreements, which cover three main areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies – were characterised by Burnham as “a good deal for Britain” and regarded as first steps towards bringing the UK back into the EU’s orbit.
Some in the UK believe that leaving the single market and customs union brought little tangible benefit while creating additional paperwork, border checks and barriers to trade with the UK’s largest export market. Others have no regrets about leaving the bloc.
According to polling expert Sir John Curtice, surveys show an average of 62 percent favour rejoining, against 38 percent for staying out, once undecided respondents are excluded.
“Whatever the nuances, the UK public are certainly in a different place on the EU than [they were] in 2016,” he told Al Jazeera.
According to some analysts, the government – which is not bound by a single written constitution – could, with the EU’s agreement, begin the process of rejoining without holding another referendum, or even including the commitment in an election manifesto.
However, doing so would inevitably be politically difficult and, according to Professor Curtice, almost certain to be highly unpopular.
“The Brexit referendum in 2016 was not legally binding,” Sionaidh Douglas-Scott, the chair in Law at Queen Mary University of London, wrote by email. “Legally, it could have been ignored altogether. But it was thought to be politically unacceptable to ignore the public’s vote in the referendum. And political parties can ignore their election manifesto pledges at their peril,” she said, referring to parties’ reliance on public trust to support any agenda.
“I suspect Burnham might be tempted to have a referendum on the issue of rejoining the EU, feeling that public opinion had changed sufficiently to render a rejoin vote likely, although that’s by no means certain,” she said. “Some senior members of the [governing Labour] party … clearly feel that rejoining should be a manifesto pledge. So, politically, steps might be taken to make it more acceptable.”
Meanwhile, questions remained over the terms on which the UK might rejoin the bloc, whether it would be required to adopt the euro – a prospect it had previously resisted – and what form the EU itself might take following elections in some of its most influential member states, including France, Germany and Spain.
Polling suggests a distinction between support for closer relations with the EU as opposed to support for full membership.
While some surveys put support for rejoining at about 35 percent when closer ties were offered as an alternative, Curtice said support for closer relations was often less firmly held.
“Much of that support is soft – people say they somewhat support rather than strongly support” closer ties, he explained. By contrast, around half of those supporting rejoining the EU say they “strongly support” it, suggesting a deeper commitment to that option.
Similarly, at home, many of the more prominent figures of the original campaign to leave Europe have resurfaced and appear to be marshalling their forces against any return or realignment.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of Brexit’s most prominent campaigners, returned to Brussels on Thursday to oppose the prime minister’s efforts.
Other figures associated with the Leave campaign have also re-emerged, including former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and his former cabinet ally, Michael Gove, now a magazine editor. They have revived loosely sourced claims about the financial cost of rejoining the EU – or even of having remained a member. The campaign group Stay Out, for instance, puts the annual cost at 39.3 billion pounds (approximately $51.4bn), equivalent to 750 million pounds (about $982m) a week.
“I think we should think about two things when we think about Brexit and the potential to rejoin: trauma and salience,” Anand Menon, professor at King’s College London and director of UK in a Changing Europe, said. “Some people felt traumatised by the first debate and don’t want to revisit it. At the same time, the issue has lost its salience. The public don’t consider it one of the main issues facing the country,” he said.
“If you cast your mind back to 2016, those supporting Leave, like Nigel Farage, took the EU, which the public never really thought about, and linked it in the public’s mind to something they absolutely did: immigration.
“If Burnham is going to try to get the sort of energy he’ll need to see the process through, he’s going to need to do something similar, though what, I don’t know.”

Warehouses, railway stations, energy plants and residential buildings were hit during a night of heavy Russian strikes
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".
The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.
At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.
The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
At least two people were killed in a strike on a railway station in western Ukraine
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.
The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit €70bn (£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.
The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.
On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country .
It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.
Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.
Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.
France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.
He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan on Friday to shutter the notorious Rikers Island jail by the end of 2032, proposing to push the deadline from August 2027.
Rikers, long criticised for unsanitary conditions and violence, is due to be replaced by four borough-based jails as part of an effort to improve safety and tackle overcrowding.
The four new sites will be set in the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan and Queens, with the Brooklyn facility scheduled to open in 2029.
The plan aims to bring facilities closer to courts, families and public transportation, while also reducing detention and case delay to help bring the jail population down from around 6,600 people to no more than 4,100 by the end of 2032.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement released on Friday.
“For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane," he continued. "This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprives people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146 million in evidence-based supports that help break the cycles of incarceration."
"We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers," he added.
Rikers had been slated to close by August 2027 following legislation passed by the City Council in 2019. Moving the deadline will require a change to this law.
"Year after year, Rikers has taken a toll," Mamdani said in a press conference on Friday. "It has made us less safe. Because it has hollowed out those we love and failed those who need help. And because it has endured as a blight almost since the year it was built. A place we have long turned our eyes from rather than confront head on."
"Today, we lead differently. I am proud that New York City will close Rikers Island once and for all," he added.

The plan would replace the jail complex with four smaller jails and reduce the number of people behind bars.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a plan to close the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, setting out how his administration hopes to shut down a facility long criticised for violence, overcrowding and poor sanitation.
The plan, released on Friday, proposes closing the jail five years after a deadline of August 2027 that was set under then-Mayor Bill de Blasio.
With less than a year to go, the four smaller jails in four New York boroughs that are meant to replace Rikers are still under construction.
The jail complex mostly holds people awaiting trial rather than serving sentences after conviction.
“For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane,” said Mamdani in a statement.
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” he said.
The mayor’s strategy involves reducing the number of people held at Rikers from 6,700 to no more than 4,100 by expanding alternatives to detention, restoring online bail payments, investing in programmes that aim to reduce repeat offending, and shortening court delays.
Court delays can leave people “detained for years in what is essentially legal purgatory”, said Mamdani at a news conference on Friday. The city plans to set up a task force to deal with bottlenecks and improve how agencies share evidence.
Under the new timeline, the first replacement jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, with the rest completed by 2032. The city plans to also make hospital beds available for people in custody who have serious mental health or medical needs.
“Any family member of someone held at Rikers will tell you how isolating that jail is, how it can take hours to visit a loved one,” Mamdani said, adding that the new jails would be closer to courts and public transport, and would help integrate imprisoned New Yorkers back into the city.
Rikers Island, near LaGuardia airport in New York’s East River, opened in 1932 and has long faced criticism over violence, abuse, and unsanitary conditions, with campaigners pushing for its closure for over a decade.
The facility has been tied to cases like that of Kalief Browder, who spent three years there awaiting trial before the charges against him were dismissed. He died by suicide in 2015 aged 22, two years after his release.
City lawmakers voted to close Rikers in 2019, and Mamdani has blamed the city’s inability to meet the 2027 deadline to build the replacement jails on the previous administration.
Once the jail closes, Mamdani said he wants the island to be used for renewable energy and projects to help the city withstand the effects of climate change.
“Our hope is that the new Rikers Island will be unrecognisable,” he said.

Island Global Research said the survey was completed by more than 3,000 people across Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man
There has been "a major increase" in the overall cost of living in the past 12 months in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man, a survey has found.
Island Global Research, a market research and consultancy company, found more than 69% of respondents in Jersey, 68% in Guernsey and 70% in the Isle of Man said they had noticed a cost increase , external .
The survey, which was completed by over 1,000 people in each island, saw 57% of respondents describe themselves as "less than comfortable" with about one in 10 going without essentials like food and heating.
The survey also found 65% said they now spent less on non essentials and 53% said they are shopping around more because of the price rises.
In Jersey, 10% of respondents reported they could not afford the increased costs and often have to go with out essentials, while in Guernsey it was 11%.
The survey also showed that two thirds of people in Jersey said they had found it difficult to meet living costs in the last 12 months, an increase of 17 percentage points compared to 2024 .
Guernsey also saw an increase with 58% reporting they found it difficult to meet living costs.
The survey also found about one in four received support to help finance their everyday living expenses in the last six months.
On the Isle of Man, 36% said they cut back on groceries and 30% received support to help finance everyday living expenses over a six-month period.

The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.
But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.
That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.
However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.
Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.
Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.
That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating.
Protesters have rallied across 25 European countries amid a wave of public discontent over issues ranging from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people.
Inspired by demonstrations that have shaken France in recent months, thousands took to the streets in countries including the United Kingdom, Austria, Germany, Spain, Italy, Sweden and Croatia on Friday.
Tens of thousands of workers and students protested in more than 100 Italian cities to demand higher wages ⁠⁠and greater investment in public services.
The rallies coincided with a general strike by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL, that involved workers in ‌‌both the private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare.
“Across Europe and among ordinary people, the demand for change is growing,” CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said at a rally in Rome.
Demonstrators in Rome threw objects at the Ministry of Education, while in Bologna some protesters clashed with police, news agency ANSA reported. In Milan, demonstrators set fire to a cardboard tanker as well as cardboard figures depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and United States President Donald Trump.
The Italian rallies ⁠⁠followed a nationwide mobilisation on October 17 that descended into rioting and looting and prompted the right-wing government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to approve sweeping security measures and deploy the army alongside police in subsequent demonstrations.
Student groups have since continued protests and occupations at schools and universities, with opposition to higher military spending also emerging as a rallying cry.
Opposition leaders joining demonstrations on Friday criticised Meloni’s government and its budget policies amid rising living costs. Elly Schlein, leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, said the 2027 Budget Law “does not have a vision for the future of the country” as it does not help industries but slashes funding for public healthcare and education.
Meanwhile, in Germany, campaign group “Gen Z regelt” (German for “Gen Z sorts it”) said it ⁠⁠was organising protests in 73 cities and towns.
In Berlin, roughly 4,000 people attended a protest in the city’s ⁠⁠Alexanderplatz square.
The Cologne protest drew fewer than the 5,000 people expected, though ⁠⁠demonstrators still numbered in the thousands, police said.
Protesters gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service.
In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.
In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.
Demonstrations across Europe were inspired by much larger protests in France that began in September and descended into violent confrontations with the police and looting.
On Tuesday, France’s Interior Ministry said a total of 146,000 people took part in protests across the country , with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency.
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 percent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 percent in Spain, 11 percent in France and 20 percent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.

Chants of "shame, shame, shame" echoed through a packed press conference as climate campaigners fiercely rejected the draft negotiating text on the scheduled final day of the two-week United Nations climate summit . Organised by Climate Action Network (CAN) International , the briefing saw delegates and activists applaud speakers who accused governments of failing to tackle fossil fuel dependence, spanning coal, oil and gas, or build on pledges made at last year’s summit in Belém, Brazil .
CAN executive director Tasneem Essop urged nations, particularly across the Global South , to walk away from the current text, while the network’s acting head of global political strategy, Anabella Rosemberg , warned: "We will fight back, and we say thank you for nothing." Questioning how COP31 could be judged a success without tangible progress over the past 12 months , Power Shift Africa director Mohamed Adow echoed wider anger that the talks had sidelined the priorities of climate-vulnerable states.
With the United States, one of the world’s top greenhouse gas emitters, absent for a second consecutive year , nearly 200 participating countries remained deadlocked over a final declaration whose commitments largely stay voluntary and non-binding, raising the prospect that negotiations could spill well past Friday’s official closing deadline.

Chambers left Aranjuez prison near Madrid on Friday afternoon, shortly after Spain’s High Court ordered him released.
A court in Spain has granted conditional bail to James “Fergie” Chambers, a pro-Palestine philanthropist who is the subject of an ongoing extradition request by the United States government.
Chambers left Aranjuez prison near Madrid on Friday afternoon, shortly after Spain’s High Court ordered him released. Speaking to journalists outside the prison, Chambers thanked his supporters.
“I got letters from all over the place these past months. People who don’t know me across Spain,” he told reporters. “I am grateful for the people of this country”.
Chambers said his mother was visiting him in the prison today when they were told, saying “we were sitting and eating some cookies and the guards knocked on my door and said give us five minutes we have some good news for you”. He said it was a “sweet moment” finding out he was going to be released while his mother was visiting him and that he will now have time with his mother who is visiting Spain, adding “this is very special,” said Chambers.
Chambers’s legal team described the bail release as “wonderful news”.
“My client has been imprisoned for nearly five months without having been convicted of any crime, and in the absence of credible evidence to support the US charges. We hope the National Court will reject this baseless extradition request,” said Aitor Martinez, Chambers’s lawyer, in a statement.
The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas. He is not charged with any “terrorism” offences and denies any wrongdoing.
Chambers’ wife Stella Schnabel said: “Today is an enormous relief. After nearly five months of only being able to see Fergie through a pane of glass during prison visits, and our five year old son asking every day where his dad is, we can finally be together as a family. Nothing can undo what we have endured, or the time Fergie has lost with our son, but at least we can now be together.
“But we still have a cloud of uncertainty hanging over us. Fergie faces the threat of extradition to the US, where he risks up to 30 years in prison for his solidarity with the Palestinian people. Our baby is due in March, and we have no idea whether Fergie will be by my side when our baby is born or whether he will be in a US supermax prison.”
In a recent legal development, lawyers for Chambers said mistranslations between the US criminal charge in English and the version presented to Spanish authorities in Spanish made the allegations seem more serious.
After a hearing last week, the court had been expected to rule on the extradition request in the coming weeks, but it said on Friday that the translation errors could delay a final decision.
The High Court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent’s sworn statement, submitted in support of the extradition request.
“The US authorities’ admission that they made ‘substantial’ changes to the extradition documents when translating them into Spanish raises grave concerns that the evidence was manipulated to mislead the Spanish authorities about the seriousness of the allegations against my client,” said Martinez.
“This further demonstrates why the UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders has warned that Fergie would face ‘irreparable human rights violations’ if extradited to the US and has called for the extradition request to be rejected.”
Chambers, the heir to the Cox Enterprises media fortune and worth a reported $250m, was arrested on an Interpol Red Notice in Ibiza in July, but has since applied for asylum in Spain.
He cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited from Spain to the US at all.
Chambers’s wife, Stella Schnabel, previously told Al Jazeera that she was appealing to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to intervene on their behalf and grant an expedited asylum request.
“If [Sanchez] chooses not to act, he risks enabling [US President Donald] Trump to establish a precedent in Spain and across Europe which criminalises solidarity with the Palestinian people,” she said.

Nikhil Gupta (seen in a 2024 courtroom sketch) pleaded guilty in a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a U.S. resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.
Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.
US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.
Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".
India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.
At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.
"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.
Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."
Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader
India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.
In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."
